Yes, flowers did exist during the age of dinosaurs. Research from Harvard University, reported by both Reuters and ScienceDaily, found that orchids arose approximately 76–84 million years ago, making them old enough to have co-existed with dinosaurs, which went extinct around 65 million years ago [d4][d5]. Direct physical evidence from the Cretaceous period includes dinosaur coprolites (fossilized excrement) containing fragments of angiosperm (flowering plant) wood, and an ankylosaur found with angiosperm fruit in its gut [d8]. Ancient flowering plants with fragrant scents have been found preserved in amber dating back as far as 100 million years, during the Cretaceous period when dinosaurs were abundant [d6]. In fact, one study from Murdoch University found a flower fossil from the Rhamnaceae (buckthorn) family to be approximately 260 million years old, suggesting flowering plants may have predated dinosaurs entirely [d3]. The oldest known flower fossils more broadly date to the Early Cretaceous period, around 140 million years ago, and the Mesozoic Era — the Age of Dinosaurs — is recognized as including the appearance of the first flowers [d1][d7].
